## Recovery Continues in Q4, But Still a Long Way to Go 



- The recovery that we saw beginning in Q3 at a global level has continued in Q4 with copper cable consumption falling by 3.5% in Q4 compared to 4.4% in Q3. Of course Q4 2008 was very weak, and this has helped the year-on-year comparison, but we believe that the recovery is gaining strength, although there is clearly a very long way still to go. 



- The patchy nature of the recovery continues with growth in China continuing strongly and this driving an improving picture in North East Asia. For North America and Europe the market remains slow, with only very patchy signs of a recovery. As a result industry rationalisation is continuing, particularly in Europe, and consequently when the recovery does gather pace local copper rod capacity may not be enough to meet demand, which is likely to lead to rising imports. 



- It’s still too early in 2010 for most industry players to form any clear view about how the new year will develop, although the very weak nature of Q1 2009 means that for many countries year-on-year comparisons could well turn positive for the first time since Q3 2008. The winding wire sector is forecast to be amongst the first to return to growth in 2010, whilst the market for cables used in the construction industry is expected to remain slow through most of this year.

© 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 12 January 2010 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # Europe According to our estimates, copper wirerod production in Europe totalled 611,000 tonnes in Q4 2009, down by 19.3% from the same period of the previous year. For the full 2009 we have estimated that output reached 2,715,000 tonnes, a 21.7% year-on-year contraction. Our numbers indicate that copper wire and cable production in Europe amounted to 490,000 tonnes in Q4 2009, down from 594,000 tonnes in Q4 2008. Production in 2009 is estimated to have been 2,147,000 tonnes; that was a 23.6% year-onyear decline. CRU’s contacts have reported that this early in the year they remain uncertain whether a change in the economic climate has actually taken place. There are mixed market rumours about wirerod plant closures and financial difficulties. We have been told that certain non-vertically integrated producers face problems that could lead to further changes in the industry, with Cuprom in Romania reportedly in difficulties. On a positive note, following the restructuring that took place in 2009, particularly the cuts in human resources, European companies are now in a far stronger position to face the market challenges. Given the severe demand downturn that occurred in 2009, the market remains cautious about 2010 and waits for Q1 to provide some indication for the rest of the year. In particular, the market does not know how major end-users, such as the automotive and white appliances sectors, will perform. Will the recovery signs felt in H2 2009 - supported mainly by the stimulus packages - be sustained onto 2010? ### **The European region in numbers** Our findings suggest that copper wirerod production in **Germany** contracted by 16.9% in 2009 to an estimated 673,000 tonnes. While all quarters were down year-on-year, the steepest fall was seen in Q1 which declined by 29.3%. The contraction rate fell to 10.1% year-on-year in Q4, backed by promising recovery signs in this major European market. In **France** , 2009 copper wirerod production shrunk by 28.2% to 232,000 tonnes. Output in Q4 plunged by 41.9% to an estimated 38,000 tonnes, after **Nexans** announced the closure of its **Chauny** plant. **Italian** production of copper wirerod is anticipated to have dropped by 15.7% to 387,000 tonnes in 2009. Noticeable was the plunge in **Russian** output of copper wirerod. We estimate that Russian production plummeted by 40.8% year-on-year to 410,000 tonnes in 2009. This major downturn was reflected both in exports and domestic wirerod consumption too. Russian exports of copper wirerod are projected to have fallen

by 50% to 193,000 tonnes whilst domestic consumption appeared to have decreased by 29.7% to 220,000 tonnes in 2009. **Aurubis** reported that in the FY ended September 2009, copper wirerod output amounted to 622,000 tonnes, down by 13.4% from the previous year. The company attributed that to reduced market demand, particularly in the first half, and commented that the trend was reversed from summer 2009 onwards with a slow but steady increase in demand. **Nexans** published an 18.9% organic drop in its cable business for Q3 2009, compared to a 16.4% contraction seen in H1 2009. As the company remarked there was no ‘marked deterioration or noteworthy improvement either’. **Prysmian** said that in Q3 2009 it experienced a 16.0% organic decrease. The company reported that Q3 was generally weak; however, given that the organic shrinkage in H1 2009 was 18.3%, Q3 saw some indications of recovery and stabilisation. In addition, as a result of further cost reductions, **Draka** announced that it will close its LAN cable plant in **Еrnes, Norway** . |able only|||||||||||| |Data: CRU||||||||||||| © 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 5 of 12 January 2010 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # North America ### **Year ends with the first small signs of recovery** As 2009 draws to a close the North American cable industry will be glad to see the back of what turned out to be a year of unprecedented falls in demand across the whole industry. Copper wirerod production was off by 22.5% at just over 1.5 million tonnes conductor, which was 45% below the level of production in the year 2000. Copper rod consumption and wire and cable production was down by a similar percentage, with the US seeing the greatest fall with a 24.0% decline. Looking at the data on a quarterly basis there is some cause for modest optimism that the long slow road to recovery has begun, with the year-on-year fall in copper cable production in Q4 being 17.2% compared to 23%-25% in each of the first three quarters of the year. Of course Q4 2008 was very weak, but even so we should start to see a gradual improvement in year-on-year comparisons in 2010. ### **Recovery in demand from the construction sector will be quite slow** US housing constructio

n data for November shows that building permits were 6% above the October rate but 7.3% below November 2008. Housing starts were up 8.9% month-on-month but down 12.4% yearon-year. Housing completions were 8.7% up on October but 25.3% down year-on-year. It now looks as if the earliest any significant recovery in housing starts can be expected is in March 2010 and so any strong recovery in cable demand from this sector will only be seen later in 2010 and into 2011, due to the lag between starting construction and when cabling is done. In the power cable sector LV utility cables are mostly aluminium, but the MV sector uses significant volumes of copper and if there is an upturn in housing starts in March this should feed through to greater demand for these cables from utilities in Q3, although there was some overbuild that will need to work through the system. What should also provide a boost to the MV sector is the growth in investment in wind power. After a pause in 2009 due to funding issues, this looks set to increase strongly in 2010, and this will require quite large volumes of MV cable, although again there is a lag between projects being launched and cable being needed. ### **Winding wire sector should benefit from efficiency drive** The winding wire sector has been the hardest hit with regional consumption falling by 29.9% in 2009. As has been noted the weakness in the automotive and domestic appliance sectors have been the main drivers of this big drop. Now though there are a number of reasons for believing that the recovery in this sector should soon gather pace. US vehicle production is forecast to rise by 20.9% in 2010, and analysis of data on domestic appliance shipments shows that in November 2009 there was the first rise year-on-year in total shipments since July 2008, with an improving trend having started in July 2009. This growth has been driven by rising shipments of home laundry, kitchen clean up and food preservation appliances. Going forward the winding wire sector should benefit from energy efficiency regulations due to come into force at the end of 2010. This will lead to greater production of energy efficient motors with a new energy efficient motor typically using 10-20% more copper. Other new regulations are due from 2011 onwards. The wind energy sector will drive demand for large mostly taped, non-circular wires. The introduction of smart grid technology will need smart meters and more transformers which should also boost demand for winding wire, although this effect is unlikely to be significant for a number of years. © 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 6 of 12 January 2010 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** |North Americ|an coppe|r wi|re &

According to data published by the **Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association** , copper wire and cable shipments in November totalled 58,700 tonnes, down by 7.7% year-on-year.  The figure contracted by 4.7% from 61,614 tonnes in October.  November was the 14<sup>th</sup> consecutive month that deliveries fell year-on-year.  The decline was the smallest, however.  It was reported that shipments to the electrical industry declined by 2.2% year-onyear to 13,600 tonnes, but copper wire and cable sales to the construction sector fell by 12.7% year-onyear to 23,800 tonnes.  Trends show that the modest recovery in wire and cable demand is primarily being driven by the automotive and appliances sectors. However, these are not enough as the -still depressedconstruction sector accounts for half of domestic wire and cable consumption.  Moreover, market participants remain cautious about the outlook of the macroeconomic environment in Japan. 

### **South Korean strong momentum slows down in Q4 2009** 

Copper wirerod production figures suggest that South Korean output in Q4 2009 rose by 11.9% to 160,000 tonnes from the same period in 2008, following a positive annual trend from Q2 and Q3 2009. However, Q4 output fell by 7.5% from Q3.  Full 2009 South Korean production is estimated to have totalled 683,000 tonnes, an increase of 9.1% compared with 2008.  Our trade estimates show that copper wirerod exports were 164,800 tonnes in 2009, a tremendous growth of 39% year-on-year.  Shipments to China alone made up two thirds of 2009 exports; South Korean exports to China doubled in 2009.  Total exports in Q4 are anticipated to have grown by 43.8% year-on-year to 38,200 tonnes.  Domestic consumption of copper wirerod is expected to have reached 120,000 tonnes in Q4 2009, up by 1.9% yearon-year but down by 3.2% sequentially.  The strong momentum felt earlier in 2009 slowed down in Q4. 

### **Recovery signs in Taiwanese wirerod consumption, y-o-y and sequential** 

Our figures indicate that Taiwanese production of copper wirerod totalled an estimated 90,000 tonnes in Q4 2009.  The figure rose from the same period in 2008 by 6.8%, after double-digit contraction was realised in Q1-Q3.  Even though this is a recovery sign, it should be treated with caution as it is compared against a period when production had already plummeted to low levels.   Power wire and cable production in Taiwan dropped by 11.1% year-on-year to 238,100 tonnes in 2009.  Output in Q4 reached 66,975 tonnes, an increase of 19.9% from Q4 2008.   Production in December alone reached 24,360 tonnes, the highest level of the whole 2009.  Sequentially, Q4 wire and cable output rose by 3.5% quarteron-quarter.  Exports of copper wirerod in 2009 are estimated to have dropped by 28.1% year-on-year to 57,400 tonnes.  The figure in Q4 declined by 21.5% year-on-year to 11,500 tonnes.  The Taiwanese wire and cable industry was badly hit by the global economic slowdow

Q1 in which we saw a slight fall in year-on-year production, the rest of the year has proved to be very strong. In total we estimate that copper cable production grew by 11.5% to reach just over 4.4 million tonnes conductor. Copper wirerod production has grown at an even faster rate, rising by 15.0% to just over 4.3 million tonnes conductor, as rising local production has replaced some imports. The driver for this strong growth continues to be the government’s stimulus package which has boosted public infrastructure spending on railways, airports and grid expansion, plus domestic consumption of electrical appliances. We have spoken to a few of the larger cable manufacturers and some are reporting production up 25% to 35% in 2009. However, other companies are reporting smaller levels of growth, and we believe that the larger companies are gaining market share from the big group of small companies. The shortage of scrap copper has had an impact on the output of small low quality manufacturers, which use scrap as their main source of copper. 

The strongest sector continues to be power cable, but the rising price of copper is leading to some utilities, such as in Jiangsu Province, looking to increase their use of aluminium in power cables. There is still a lot of resistance to the use of aluminium in China as it is viewed as inferior to copper, but a widening price gap could erode resistance. We will be watching this issue closely through 2010. Demand for winding wire is also strong due to growth in the automotive sector and for domestic appliances for the home market. This has more than compensated for a reduction in demand for use in electrical equipment for export. With a cold winter we expect that power cable demand will soften in Q1, and some companies are already reporting a lower order book at present, but this sector should pick up in April. The winding wire sector is seeing steady demand and is also forecasting an upturn as we enter Q2. Looking further ahead the wind power sector is growing and this will require significant volumes of power cables, as will the ambitious programme to build a large number of nuclear power stations. On the downside there are worries about rising inflation and an overheating of the economy, which could cause the government to act to slow the rate of economic growth. 

### **India continues to grow and attract attention** 

The Indian market has continued to grow with GDP rising by 7.9% in Q3, with the construction sector growing by 6.5%. Industrial production grew by 9.1%, with the manufacturing sector rising by 9.3%. As a result demand for all types of wire and cable is growing, with the automotive sector being particularly strong. Car sales in November increased by 63% year-on-year, with growth of 18% from April to November. Overall we estimate that wire and cable production grew by 3.2% in 2009. © 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 11 of 12 January 2010 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # Industry News **Prysmian** has closed its acquisition of Russian cable maker **Rybinsk Electrocabel** . This company had sales of US$52m in 2008 and Prysmian intends to install facilities to make HV cables. **Draka** is to close its LAN cable plant at Еrnes in Norway. This plant employs 125 people and production will be moved to other Draka facilities in Europe. A 60ktpy copper wirerod project was kicked off on January 1 in Dafengang, Jiangsu Province. **Dafeng Port Development Co** ., Ltd and **Dafeng Juxin Metal Co** ., Ltd. have invested Yuan120m in this project. Bulgarian cable maker **Elkabel JSC** has ordered an RS 3000/6 copper rod casting machine from Rautomead. **LS Cable** has opened its newly acquired subsidiary in China which has been renamed LS Hongqi Cable Co. This company makes submarine cables and LS Cable plans an expansion to produce power and instrument and control and industrial cables. **Er-Bakir** has increased its copper rod production capacity from 108,000 tpy to 200,000 tpy with effect from mid September 2009.
